title: One Edit, Sixteen Templates
intro: The chapter above gave the counting structure of the broadcast test and the gradient the aggregate hides. This level goes under both: the arithmetic of the edit itself, the three design choices that make it a test of broadcast rather than of steering, and what the loading correlation can and cannot settle.

chapters.title: A two-number edit, held in place
chapters.body:
The [[lens-coordinate-swap]] is a two-number edit, and the arithmetic is short enough to state in full ([[eq-lens-swap]]).

Given a source token $s$ and a target token $t$, the intervention forms the matrix $V = [v_s\; v_t]$, whose two columns are the [[j-lens-vector]] for each of those tokens. It reads the activation's coordinates along them as $c = V^\dagger h$, where $h$ is the [[residual-stream]] at one position and layer.

The pseudoinverse is doing real work there ([[pseudoinverse]]). Lens vectors are neither orthogonal nor unit-norm ([[oblique-lens-coordinates]]), so the plain inner product $\langle v_s, h \rangle$ would count part of whatever $v_t$ content the activation already carries. Solving for the two coefficients together separates them.

The write-back is $h_{\text{patched}} = h + V(\sigma(c) - c)$, with $\sigma$ exchanging the two entries of $c$. Everything in $h$ orthogonal to the span of the two vectors is left exactly as it was. The edit is two dimensions wide in a residual stream of thousands.

Where the edit is applied matters as much as what it does. It goes in at every token position, across a band of middle layers ([[workspace-layers]]), and is held there for the whole forward pass rather than written once ([[activation-clamping]]).

The reason is that the prompt itself is untouched. The word France is still written in the context, and the model can read it again at any later layer. Clamping is what stops the original argument from being recomputed around the edit.

chapters.title: Three choices that make it a test of broadcast
chapters.body:
Three choices in the protocol are what make the result about broadcast rather than about steering.

The first is that the edit does not change from prompt to prompt ([[prompt-independent-swap]]). The same pair of coordinates is exchanged whether the prompt asks for a capital, a language or a continent, and nothing is fitted per template ([[function-template-protocol]]). If the France vector were legible only to the circuit that looks up capitals, one fixed edit would redirect that template and leave the others alone. [[fig-18]] is the worked case: three templates, one edit, three answers that all move to the swapped-in country.

The second is that the target is drawn from the same category as the source ([[swap-target-selection]]). A month swapped into "the capital of ___ is" would leave no target-appropriate answer to score against, so the four arguments of a category are only ever exchanged with each other.

The third is the scoring rule, and it carries the argument. A trial counts as a success only when the model's top-1 output is the answer the template implies for the swapped-in argument ([[implied-counterfactual-answer]]) — Beijing under the capital template, not China.

That distinction is the point. A model that answered China would show only that the injected vector reached the output, which steering along a lens vector already does ([[steering-vectors]]). Answering Beijing requires some downstream circuit to have taken the vector as an argument and applied its own function to it. That is [[global-broadcast]] as the paper operationalizes it, and [[flexible-generalization]] is the property being scored.

chapters.title: What the grids print, and what a failure looks like
chapters.body:
[[fig-68]] prints every trial, and its layout is what explains the failures ([[swap-trial-grid]]).

Each function template gets a $4 \times 4$ grid. A row fixes the argument written in the prompt; a column fixes the argument whose lens coordinates are swapped in. On the diagonal the two are the same word, so the exchange is between a coordinate and itself and nothing changes ([[swap-grid-diagonal-baseline]]).

That makes the diagonal a printed baseline in the same format as the trials. It shows the model answering each template correctly with no intervention, which is what an off-diagonal failure has to be read against.

The counting follows from the shape. Sixteen cells minus four on the diagonal leaves twelve trials per grid. Four templates per category gives 48 trials per category, and four categories give the 192.

Countries reach the target answer in 42 of their 48. Number relations reach it in none of 48. Those two extremes account for 42 of the successes, so the remaining 34 fall across the 96 month and animal trials; the paper gives the ordering — months partial, animals rare — rather than the two counts.

A cell prints the model's actual top-1 token rather than a pass or a fail, with a small grey rank for the target answer when it is not first. In the failing cells that token is usually the baseline answer, with the target ranked somewhere below it.

The failure is inertia rather than noise. Elsewhere the paper reads a swap with no effect as evidence that a computation does not run through the [[j-space]] at all ([[null-swap-interpretation]]); here the same null is read as an edit that did not push hard enough. The model is Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([[claude-model-family]]).

chapters.title: Doubling the strength stops being a swap
chapters.body:
The double-strength condition is a scale factor on the correction term, and following it through shows that it is no longer an exchange ([[swap-strength-alpha]]).

The write-back becomes $h + \alpha V(\sigma(c) - c)$. At $\alpha = 1$ the source coordinate ends at $c_t$ and the target coordinate at $c_s$. That is a permutation, and the activation still sits at a point the model could have reached on some other prompt.

At $\alpha = 2$ the source coordinate ends at $c_s + 2(c_t - c_s)$, which is $2c_t - c_s$. Where the source was strongly present and the target barely present, that value is negative. The activation is carried past the exchange to a point where the source concept is present in the negative.

The two counts are therefore not two readings of one intervention. The 76 of 192 is a swap, a little under 40 percent. The 101 of 192 is a harder edit, a little over half. The property is one of the five the paper's definition names ([[workspace-like-properties]]), and it is scored on the first number.

The left panel of [[fig-19]] keeps both visible per template rather than only in aggregate ([[swap-success-chart]]): a filled circle for the default strength, a cross for double, one pair for each of the sixteen. The unit is the template, so the gain at double strength can be seen to be spread or concentrated.

One further thing the count hides is that top-1 is a threshold on something continuous. The paper's own graded quantity is how far the swap shifts the output toward the target answer ([[swap-effect-magnitude]]). A trial that lifts the target from rank 40 to rank 2 scores the same as one where nothing moved.

chapters.title: What the loading correlation settles
chapters.body:
[[workspace-loading]] is measured before any intervention, which is what makes it a predictor rather than a description of the result.

For a given trial it is the [[cosine-similarity]] between the residual stream and the source concept's lens vector, averaged over the argument and readout positions of an unmodified forward pass. No ranking over the vocabulary is involved. The lens is used here in probe form: one chosen vector, one number per position ([[j-lens-probe]]).

The right panel of the figure plots the swap's effect against that number, one point per trial. Countries load highest and move the output most; number words load lowest and move it least. The ordering of the categories in the grids and their ordering in loading are the same ordering.

What the correlation relates is worth stating carefully. Both quantities are read off the same lens vectors: loading is an inner product with $v_s$, and the swap is an edit along $v_s$ and $v_t$. A concept whose lens vector is a poor match for whatever the model actually uses would score low on both, without anything following about the model's workspace.

The paper says as much for the worst category, and stops there ([[number-word-failure-interpretation]]). The number-word failure has two readings. The model may compute over small integers outside the workspace. Or its working representation of small integers may simply not align with the lens vectors for the corresponding number tokens, since the lens is built one vector per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]] and can only name what has a single-token name ([[single-token-limitation]]).

Nothing in the loading measurement separates those two, and the paper does not claim that it does.
